newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African parties seek way to end ANC hegemony.
newsitem.headline: S.African parties seek way to end ANC hegemony.

text.p: Leaders of four South African opposition parties held two separate meetings on Tuesday but offered little hope of a strong new alliance to pose a credible challenge to the ruling African National Congress in elections just under two years away.

Tony Leon and Mangosuthu Buthelezi led delegations from the Democratic Party (DP) and the Inkatha Freedom Party in one set of talks while F.W. de Klerk, head of the National Party (Nats), met General Constand Viljoen, leader of the Freedom Front (FF).
The Nats are the biggest of the opposition groups but recent opinion polls suggest their support has dropped from around 20 percent at the time of the last election in 1994 to about 11 percent now.

The party is in turmoil following the resignation last month of Roelf Meyer, its most liberal leader, who had advocated the rapid disbandment of the Nats as the only way members could shed their image as the creators of apartheid.

Viljoen, whose party is to the right of the Nats and stands for self-determination for Afrikaners, said in a statement his hour-long meeting with de Klerk showed there were fundamental differences between them.
"No form of alliance or cooperation agreement is possible," he said. "Mr. Meyer's breakaway has begun a process of restructuring that must be approached with great responsibility."
Viljoen said the meeting had dealt with issues like constitutional goals, education, the economy, and the role of Afrikaans. "There was agreement that ad hoc cooperation was possible here," he said.
Leon, whose party represents mainly white liberals and won less than two percent of the national vote in 1994, ruled out any merger with the Zulu-based Inkatha.

"The interests of South Africa demand that two parties with as many shared values and policies should cooperate far more closely and visibly and constructively," he told reporters at the start of the talks.

Buthelezi, main black rival of President Nelson Mandela's ANC, said the meeting with the DP was not surprising because the two parties had a long history of seeing eye-to-eye on issues like federalism and a market economy.

"While it is desirable to merge -- in Africa it has been the custom since the '60s to have one-party states -- those who respect multi-party government would say it is in the interests of democracy...to have different parties," Buthelezi said.
"The existence of different political strands is in the interests of multi-party democracy."

Buthelezi said it was impractical to think a new party could be created in time to contest the 1999 election. He dismissed as over-simplification a Sunday newspaper report that quoted him as saying he wanted unity with the ANC.

Inkatha, which has a slim majority in KwaZulu-Natal province, has fought a decade-long feud with the ANC in which about 15,000 people have been killed. The violence has tapered off since 1994 but still simmers.
The ANC won 62 percent of the vote in 1994 and political analysts say it is likely to win on a similar scale in 1999.
